method.title: Latest episodes first
body: The official episode page, redbelly.network/ama, lists Episode 29 (9 July 2026) as the most recent Redbelly Insights episode. Episodes 25 to 29 were downloaded from the official links on that page and transcribed, newest first.

Only passages about Redbelly technology, Project Acacia or Tokeniser were considered. Each clip had to make one point that holds up for someone who has never heard of Redbelly, and no two clips could make the same point.

method.title: One continuous passage per clip
body: Every clip is a single uninterrupted stretch of the episode. Nothing inside a clip is cut, reordered or joined, so no quote can be edited into a different meaning.
Clips start and end on sentence boundaries, and the exact source range is listed for each clip and checked against the episode audio.

method.title: Subtitles you can trust
body: The subtitle text was proof-read word for word against three separate Whisper transcriptions (small.en, medium.en and large-v3), and every name and role was checked against official pages: redbelly.network, tokeniser.com and the guest's own company site.

Redbelly terms follow the brief: Redbelly, RBNT, Tokeniser, Project Acacia, with Australian spelling throughout. Hesitations such as "um" are left out. Subtitles are burned in, with the spoken word highlighted, and also shipped as SRT.

method.title: Speaker in shot
body: The episodes are 16:9. Each camera shot is found automatically and the speaker is located by face recognition, so the vertical window is set on the person speaking, never on the host. The window is fixed for each shot, so it never drifts or wobbles.
Where the episode itself cuts to the host for a moment, the speaker's last frame is held while the audio carries on. Those moments are listed in CLIPS.md.

method.title: Even audio, nothing added
body: Only the episode's own audio is used. Each clip is normalised with two-pass EBU R128 loudness to -14 LUFS integrated, the level X, YouTube and Instagram play at, with a peak limiter that keeps the true peak below -2 dBTP. All six sound the same.
No music, sound effects or third party material has been added.

method.title: Brand and layout
body: Clips and page follow the Redbelly DAO Task Board brand kit: slate surfaces, one red accent, Be Vietnam Pro for copy, JetBrains Mono for machine values such as episode numbers and timestamps, and the DAO logo on dark without a plate.
The hook, the speaker's name and role and the captions all sit clear of the bottom band where X, Shorts, Reels and TikTok draw their own buttons and text.

clips.hook: We spend Aussie dollars. Why settle in US dollars?
clips.speaker: Effie Dimitropoulos
clips.role_source: the episode's own on-screen title for the guest
clips.point: An Australian dollar stablecoin runs on Redbelly for sovereignty: every US dollar stablecoin is money that is not held onshore, so an Australian-built and Australian-operated chain keeps value in the local ecosystem.
clips.caption: We earn, spend and invest in Aussie dollars, so why settle digital assets in US dollars? AUDD CEO Effie Dimitropoulos on keeping money onshore with Australian-built Redbelly.
clips.text: Then why are we pushed in the digital asset space of dealing with US dollars, right? And why? Because they've been there longer, and there is that dominance, and there is that comfort. And, you know, no doubt that digital asset space is priced in US dollars. So, you know, that plays quite an important role in that. However, it all then boils down to every time you're using a US dollar, that is, and especially a US dollar stablecoin, it's money that's not sitting onshore. It's money that's not backing your asset onshore. And so supporting the Australian ecosystem by using a blockchain like Redbelly that is an Australian-built and Australian-operated blockchain is pretty important.
notes: Effie Dimitropoulos joined remotely, so the vertical window is taken from her half of the split screen. Her role is the one shown in the episode's own on-screen title.

clips.hook: Proof of stake still gets hacked. What's missing?
clips.speaker: Vincent Gramoli
clips.role: Founder & Chief Science Officer, Redbelly Network
clips.point: Proof of stake chains still get hacked. Redbelly is a regulated proof of stake chain, designed so every participant has a reason to pull in the same direction instead of tech-savvy players profiting at the expense of everyday users.
clips.caption: Proof of stake still gets hacked. Redbelly founder Vincent Gramoli on a regulated proof of stake chain where incentives line up, so tech-savvy players can't profit at everyday investors' expense.
clips.text: So it looks like, you know, blockchain has moved and matured from proof of work that was extremely energy greedy to this proof of stake strategy that is better. But still, we can see hacks happening all the time. And now we have this regulated version of proof of stake blockchain with Redbelly. I think what is extremely important is to really find a way to incentivise all the participants to go in the right direction, the same direction, right? And not to have tech-savvy people that will profit on the back of moms and pops. So really having these kind of rationals that are captured, such that everyone is doing its best so that everyone can benefit. You know, we're lowering the barrier of entry to these economic opportunities for the masses.

clips.hook: After Project Acacia, tokenised bonds are next
clips.speaker: Drew Bradford
clips.point: Tokenised bonds are the next step after Project Acacia: the RBA's Ellis Connolly named bonds as the first cab off the rank, and Brad Jones said the question is no longer if, but when and how.
clips.caption: After Project Acacia, the RBA is pointing at tokenised bonds: not if, but when and how. Macropod CEO Drew Bradford on why this is coming.
clips.text: Oh, look, we tease Brad Jones, you're not going fast enough. But look, we saw it in the budget. The only positive thing in the budget the other night was the mention of tokenised bonds, or the only positive that I talked about. So, Project Acacia, hey, you never know, it might even be out before this podcast comes out. The report, that will go through guardrails. This is where we think the market's going. Ellis Connolly, when he testified in the parliamentary economics committee, he said Project Acacia, the first cab off the rank should be bonds and tokenised bonds. Brad Jones got up the other day at the AP+ Beyond Tomorrow payments and said, you know, it's not if, it's when and how. So this is coming.
notes: For the first 1.8 seconds the episode is still on the host while Drew Bradford starts to answer, so his first frame on camera is held until the episode cuts to him. The audio is unchanged.

Names checked against official sources: Brad Jones is the RBA's Assistant Governor (Financial System) and spoke at the Australian Payments Plus (AP+) Beyond Tomorrow forum; Ellis Connolly is the RBA's Head of Payments Policy. Short host back-channel words ("yeah, yeah", "fantastic") are not subtitled.

clips.hook: Every regulated asset needs a registry. Enter Tokeniser.
clips.speaker: Alan Burt
clips.point: Every regulated asset needs a registry of who holds what, so Redbelly acquired the Liquidise registry business and rebranded it Tokeniser, covering origination, servicing and the registry before secondary trading.
clips.caption: Who holds what? In regulated markets, everything starts with the registry. Redbelly Executive Chairman Alan Burt on why Redbelly acquired Liquidise and relaunched it as Tokeniser.
clips.text: Yeah, so obviously at Redbelly, we've been always focused on how we bring financial services on chain. And Liquidise has always been a great partner of Redbelly, and they've been focused specifically at the time on private equities. We saw the opportunity at Redbelly to broaden that, and obviously focused on other alternate assets. But the key to everything is the registry. So who holds what? In a regulated environment, the bearer instrument is, other than cash, pretty much illegal now across every jurisdiction. So there is always regulatory required a registry. And so we've been working with Matt and saw the opportunity with some of our other partners to greatly accelerate that adoption by helping them with already having a tokenised registry. So as Matt said, we've acquired Liquidise, the registry business and their customers, and we've now rebranded that into Tokeniser, which is much more focused on a full cradle to grave, if you like, on asset origination, asset servicing and obviously registry, and then what everyone wants to hear about, the secondary trading opportunities that will be unlocked. But we've got to start with, let's get the assets on.
notes: Subtitle decision at 27 s: the three transcription models split between "regularly" and "regulatory" required. The subtitle follows large-v3 and the sense of the sentence, which is about what regulation requires.

clips.hook: What Project Acacia tested inside a real fund
clips.speaker: Matt Mills
clips.point: In Project Acacia, Tokeniser used a real fund, with TAF Capital as trustee and Macropod's AUDM stablecoin for settlement, to run subscriptions, distributions and redemptions in fully tokenised form.
clips.caption: A real fund, a real stablecoin, three everyday fund processes. Tokeniser's Matt Mills on what Project Acacia tested, and why tokenised fund processes are quicker, safer and more transparent.
clips.text: So Tokeniser had the privilege of also being involved in Project Acacia. We had the benefit of working with both the trustee, TAF Capital, who were fantastic partners in letting us essentially use one of their funds as a guinea pig for the purpose of Project Acacia, and Macropod, who supplied and provided the AUD stablecoin, AUDM, infrastructure for which we could settle against any transactions. So one of the cool things that Tokeniser did was essentially, as rightly pointed out, tackle some of those processes and payments in a fully tokenised fashion. And the goal was to demonstrate just how much quicker, safer and more transparent those processes would be in a tokenised fashion versus a traditional style. So to give an example, we tried to essentially conduct three normal, common processes that exist in any fund. Those were the subscriptions: how does an investor acquire the units? They were the distributions and the redemptions.
notes: For the first 0.7 seconds the episode is still on the host while Matt Mills starts to answer, so his first frame on camera is held until the episode cuts to him. The audio is unchanged.
TAF Capital was the trustee of the Project Acacia fund, and Macropod issues the AUDM stablecoin used for settlement.

clips.hook: What investors see when they log in to Tokeniser
clips.speaker: Matt Mills
clips.point: Tokeniser gives investors a familiar web portal: log in, see holdings and their value, download statements and certificates and receive announcements, which makes the issuer look serious and puts investors first.
clips.caption: Log in, see your holdings, download your statements. Tokeniser's Matt Mills on why tokenised assets should feel like a modern investor portal, and why investors are the real customers.
clips.text: And from a user experience, it's very much that traditional web experience. You get invited to view your holdings in a particular company or fund. You register an account, you log in and have a dashboard where you can see your holdings, see the value of those holdings. You can download statements, whether they're holding statements, share certificates, unit certificates, receive communications in the form of announcements or communications from the company or funds. And what's nice about that, and the user feedback we've gotten from our existing clients, has been that it's modern, it's fast, and most importantly, it looks and makes the issuer look serious, and shows that they care about the investor experience. And that's something that really matters to us, because we know that at the end of the day, even though it's the trustees or the companies that pay our fees and subscribe or use the product, they're doing it for the benefit of their investors. And we know our real customers are those investors, and getting a really good experience.
notes: From 49.8 s to 52.1 s of the clip (episode 24:03.5 to 24:05.9) the episode cuts away from Matt Mills, so his last frame is held with a slow push-in while the audio carries on.
